Pd-catalyzed regioselective synthesis of allenyl
sulfones via sulfinate-enabled isomerization
Cite this: Chem. Commun., 2026,
Shiwen Fan,<sup>a</sup> Zhaoqiang Chen,<sup>a</sup> Wenya Li,<sup>a</sup> Hui Qian *<sup>a</sup> and Shengming Ma *<sup>ab</sup>
Received 21st April 2026,
Accepted 30th May 2026
rsc.li/chemcomm
An eficient Pd-catalyzed C–S coupling strategy for the synthesis of
tetrasubstituted allenyl sulfones has been developed. Excess sulfinate
uniquely acts as both coupling partner and isomerization promoter,
driving the in situ generated propargyl sulfone to allenyl sulfone
conversion with a high regioselectivity and a broad substrate scope.
Organosulfone compounds, valued for their unique physicochem-
ical properties, are prevalent in natural products and bioactive
molecules.<sup>1</sup> Their stability, synthetic accessibility,<sup>2</sup> and diverse
reactivity enable participation in key transformations such as
Julia–Kocienski olefination,<sup>3</sup> Claisen rearrangement,<sup>4</sup> and Truce–
Smiles rearrangement.<sup>5</sup> Furthermore, they undergo desulfonylative
conversions via transition metal catalysis, organocatalysis, photo-
catalysis, or electrocatalysis.<sup>6</sup> Consequently, the synthesis of sulfone
compounds has attracted significant interest, driving the develop-
ment of numerous methods.<sup>7</sup> Allenyl sulfones, a distinct subclass
that retains sulfonyl functionality while incorporating allene
groups, are versatile building blocks in organic synthesis.<sup>8</sup> There-
fore, the development of efficient synthetic methods to access
allenyl sulfones has attracted considerable scientific interest.<sup>9</sup>
In prior work, our group established a methodology for the
synthesis of allenes via SO extrusion in the transition-metal-
catalyzed reaction of propargylic alcohol derivatives with sodium
sulfinates (Scheme 1a).<sup>10</sup> Nevertheless, the synthesis of allenyl
sulfones poses significant challenges in both chemoselectivity
and regioselectivity. In this context, we report a Pd-catalyzed C–S
coupling between propargylic acetates and sodium sulfinates.
This reaction affords tetrasubstituted allenyl sulfones with an
excellent regioselectivity and a broad functional group tolerance
under mild conditions.
Our study initiated with the reaction of propargylic acetate
1a and sodium p-toluenesulfinate 2a. Employing Pd<sub>2</sub>(dba)<sub>3</sub>-
CHCl as catalyst in a DMF/H O mixed solvent at 100 1C for
16 h, the reaction aforded the product 3aa in 76% yield (Table 1,
entry 1. For detailed ligand screening, see supplementary infor-
mation (SI) Table S1). Systematic optimization of the reaction
conditions was focused on solvent, reaction time, and palladium
source. The reactions in other mixed solvents of DMA or dioxane
with water led to reduced yields (Table 1, entries 2 and 3).
However, the reaction in DMSO/H O aforded the 3aa in an
improved yield of 79% (Table 1, entry 4). Reducing the reaction
time to 1 h achieved a complete conversion with an 81% yield
(Table 1, entry 5). While other Pd sources aforded comparable
results (Table 1, entries 6 and 7), utilizing Pd (dba) significantly
enhanced the yield to 91% (Table 1, entry 8). Control experiments
confirmed the essential role of palladium, as no reaction
occurred in its absence (Table 1, entry 9). Omission of the ligand
or water resulted in diminished yields (64% and 53%, respec-
tively) and the detection of by-product propargylic sulfone 4aa
(Table 1, entries 10 and 11). Upon running the reaction on
1 mmol, an 80% yield of 3aa was obtained (Table 1, entry 12).
Notably, replacement of
\mathrm { P d } _ { 2 } ( \mathrm { d b a } ) _ { 3 }
with Pd(dmdba) under the
otherwise same conditions further improved the yield to 87%
(Table 1, entry 13). Consequently, the optimized conditions for
further study were defined as follows: 1a (1.0 mmol), 2a (2.2 equiv.),
a) Transition metal-catalyzed coupling of propargylic alcohol derivatives with sodium sulfinates
b) Pd-catalyzed coupling of propargylic acetates with sodium sulfinates (this work)
Scheme 1 Previous work and our strategy for the synthesis of allenyl
sulfones.

With the optimized reaction conditions, we evaluated the
substrate scope using diverse propargylic acetates and sodium
sulfinates (Scheme 2). The substrates with either electron-donating
(1b–1f) or electron-withdrawing (1g–1j) groups on the aryl rings
(Ar) reacted smoothly with p-toluenesulfinate 2a, affording the
corresponding allenyl sulfones 3ba–3ja smoothly. Single-crystal
X-ray diffraction of 3ea unambiguously confirmed the product
structures. Notably, steric effects exerted minimal influence: ortho-
methyl (1b), meta-methyl (1c), and para-methyl (1d) substrates all
delivered products 3ba–3da with comparable yields. Similarly,
2-(naphth-2-yl)oct-3-yn-2-yl acetate (1k) provided 3ka in 72% yield.
Substitution patterns at
\mathbf { R } ^ { 1 }
were also explored: aryl-substituted
substrates 1l–1n generated allenyl sulfones 3la-3n in moderate
yields, while the substrates with alkyl chains of varying lengths
(1o–1r) consistently produced the corresponding allenes 3oa-3ra.
The deuteromethylated analogue 1s furnished deuterated product
3sa in an excellent yield. Then, we examined the
substituent: a
series of substrates containing reactive functional groups and
varying carbon chain lengths reacted smoothly, yielding moderate
to good results (3ta-3Ba). When propargylic acetate 1A bearing a
terminal chloro group was employed, the disulfone product 3Aa
was obtained via Pd-catalyzed sulfonylation and nucleophilic
substitution. Aryl
\mathbf { R } ^ { 2 }
groups (1C–1F) were also tolerated (3Ca–
3Fa). Finally, pharmaceutically relevant fragments from probene-
cid, febuxostat, adapalene (1G–1I) were successfully incorporated,
delivering allenes 3Ga–3Ia in moderate yields. The present reaction
conditions show limitations in preparation of di- and trisubsti-
tuted allenyl sulfones (see Scheme S1 in SI for details).

H O (2.5/0.25 mL) at 100 1C under Ar atmosphere. <sup>a</sup>Pd(dmdba) (7.5 mol%),
DPEphos (9 mol%) was used. <sup>b</sup>1 (2.0 mmol) was used. <sup>c</sup>Pd(dmdba) (7.5 mol%),
DPEphos (9 mol%), DMSO/H O (2.5/0.5 mL) was used. <sup>d</sup>2 (4.4 equiv.),
Pd(dmdba) (7.5 mol%), DPEphos (9 mol%) was used. <sup>e</sup>1 (2.0 mmol),
Pd(dmdba) (7.5 mol%), DPEphos (9 mol%) was used.
We next examined the scope of sodium sulfinates (Scheme 3).
Aryl sodium sulfinates reacted smoothly with propargylic acetates,
afording allenyl sulfones 3ab–3ae in moderate to good yields.
Critically, all substrates delivered comparable results as compared
to p-toluenesulfinate 2a, indicating minimal electronic influence.
2-Naphthalenesulfonyl and pyridine-3-sulfonyl variants also parti-
cipated efficiently, yielding 3Kf and 3ag in moderate yields. The
alkyl sodium sulfinates, including methyl, isopropyl and cyclopro-
pyl, also demonstrate decent reactivity (3mh–3mj).
To highlight the synthetic utility, a gram-scale reaction deliv-
ered 1.0321 g of 3ya (55% yield, Scheme 4). Under the Cu catalysis,
3ya underwent C–S bond functionalization with Grignard reagents
to construct a C–C bond.<sup>11</sup> Subsequent desilylation with TBAF
afforded allenol 4 in 50% yield over two steps. Alternatively, direct
desilylation of 3ya efficiently provided allenol 5 with a yield of

Based on mechanistic studies, we have proposed a catalytic
cycle (Scheme 6): propargylic acetate 1 undergoes oxidative addi-
tion with Pd(0), predominantly forming propargyl-palladium(II)
complex I alongside a minor amount of allenyl-palladium(II)
isomer
\mathbf { I ^ { \prime } } . ^ { 1 3 }
In the dominant pathway, subsequent ligand exchan-
ging with sodium sulfinate 2 afords intermediate II, which
undergoes reductive elimination to deliver propargylic sulfone 4
while regenerating Pd(0). Intermediate alkyne product 4 then re-
enters the catalytic cycle via oxidative addition to regenerate
propargylic palladium complex II, and there are two possible

Mechanistic investigation commenced with the monitoring of
the reaction of propargylic acetate 1a and sodium p-toluenesulfinate
2a under the standard conditions (Scheme 5a). Within 2.5 minutes,
1a underwent 85% conversion, yielding propargylic sulfone 4aa as
the primary intermediate (78%) alongside minimal allenyl
sulfone 3aa (8%). Complete substrate depletion at 5 minutes
aforded alkyne 4aa (65%) and allene 3aa (16%), confirming
concurrent isomerization of alkyne 4aa to allene 3aa. This trans-
formation progressed continuously until exclusive formation of
3aa at 50 minutes with 82% yield. Control experiments established
the essential role of palladium: 4aa remained inert without the Pd
catalyst (eqn (1) in Scheme 5b). Omission of 2a permitted only
partial isomerization to 3aa (Scheme 5b, eqn (2)), whereas
inclusion of Pd and 2a drove complete conversion to 3aa even
with 10 mol% of sulfinate 2a (Scheme 5b, eqn (3)), demonstrat-
ing its dual function as a reactant and an isomerization
promoter.

Based on mechanistic studies, we have proposed a catalytic
cycle (Scheme 6): propargylic acetate 1 undergoes oxidative addi-
tion with Pd(0), predominantly forming propargyl-palladium(II)
complex I alongside a minor amount of allenyl-palladium(II)
isomer
\mathbf { I ^ { \prime } } . ^ { 1 3 }
In the dominant pathway, subsequent ligand exchan-
ging with sodium sulfinate 2 afords intermediate II, which
undergoes reductive elimination to deliver propargylic sulfone 4
while regenerating Pd(0). Intermediate alkyne product 4 then re-
enters the catalytic cycle via oxidative addition to regenerate
propargylic palladium complex II, and there are two possible
pathways for the conversion of intermediate II to allenyl sulfone
3: Path 1 involves concerted
\mathrm { S } _ { \mathrm { N } } 2 ^ { \prime }
displacement by sulfinate 2,
directly yielding 3 and releasing Pd(0); Path 2 proceeds via direct
isomerization of II to allenyl-palladium(II) complex III, followed
by reductive elimination to furnish 3 and Pd(0), thereby complet-
ing the catalytic cycle. Direct conversion via I<sup>0</sup> cannot be excluded
as supported by the fact that a trace amount of 3 was formed at 2.5
minutes (Scheme 5a).

In summary, we have established an eficient Pd-catalyzed
C–S bond formation strategy for synthesizing tetrasubstituted
allenyl sulfones. Critical to this methodology is the use of
excess sodium sulfinate, which drives the isomerization of
propargyl sulfone intermediates to the target allenyl sulfones.
This approach delivers an exceptional regioselectivity and a
broad substrate scope, encompassing diverse functional groups
and pharmaceutical motifs. Our laboratory is currently con-
ducting further research on this topic.
